meta.title: GLM 5.2 and the coming AI margin collapse
meta.author: martinald

comments.author: df
comments.text:
The pricing math is interesting, and less in GLM's favor than you might think.

For coding, the dominant cost is input tokens. Most providers offer a 90% discount on cached input tokens, with an LRU cache that lasts 5 minutes typically. So cost is all about maximizing your use of the cache and putting in new input tokens as infrequently as possible. Claude Code is made by Anthropic, so it can be very smart about doing this.

Model routing also enables significant cost reductions. They likely have quantized versions of the models that are 95% as good but far cheaper to run, and use them without necessarily informing you.

Based on some reverse engineering, users have discovered that Claude Code has a 36x discount over API prices. That is, for your $100/month fee, you get $3600 equivalent of API usage. This is presumably because Anthropic has figured out some clever things to do with model routing and input caching, and also can subsidize with investor money and take a hit on their operating margins.

Using the 36x discount, GLM would have to be 1/36th the price of Claude to beat it on cost. In reality it is about 1/4th to 1/8th depending on the provider you use. GLM would need to replicate some of the cost-saving measures that Anthropic has figured out, which requires tight integration between the model, the provider, and the coding harness.

In non-coding usage, like processing documents or doing chat support, GLM might still come out cheaper.

Personally, I used GLM 5.2 for a project last night, and spent $4.76 in a couple hours of messing around using an ultra-cheap provider. If I did that every day, it wouldn't be too hard to exceed Claude Code's $100/month tier.

comments.author: df
comments.text:
Some other possibilities:


They expect you to pay $100/month, and only use a small fraction of your quota. One hint is that the 20x plan is more expensive per-token than the 5x plan - because if you buy the 20x plan,  you're likely actually using it heavily, while perhaps some people pay $100/month and are light users.

They may have set their API rates as a starting point for negotiation, and they were greatly inflated from the start. Much like AWS charges very high prices for bandwidth, but drops them by 90% or more for customers with a negotiated discount.

They are expecting to greatly decrease costs or increase prices in the future, and plan to get users hooked today while taking a loss. Many tech companies lost money for the first few decades of their existence while building scale, and then "flipped the switch" to raise prices and turn a profit.


Without working there, it's all speculation.

comments.author: teoruiz
comments.text:
The important point is that the $100 or $200 monthly plans are not available to a large number of customers (enterprises, and generally any company with >150 seats), who pay pure token-based API prices. Same goes for non-agentic-coding usage of LLMs through the API.

That's why I think open-weights like GLM will be used heavily by many companies, and in fact already are (a recent public example is Coinbase).

comments.author: df
comments.text: (In the long run though, it's a whole lot easier to develop cost-saving measures on top of LLMs, than to create the LLMs in the first place. So I expect the open architectures will catch up. It may just take a while since no one really has the incentive to do it currently.)

comments.author: refi64
comments.text:
I'm a certified Open Weight Models Endorser, but there are a few missed things in here:


In terms of subscriptions, Z.ai offers a "coding plan" subscription which mirrors the plans you'd see from Anthropic and OpenAI, but with a higher claimed usage limit.


If you poke around a bit on e.g. the subreddit or Twitter, it's filled with a great many complaints about heavy rate-limiting and inconsistent performance. Z.ai is generally just pretty compute-starved, so although 5.2 seems to be faring a bit better on average than 5.1 did (based on misc feedback I've observed), I don't think this plan is really comparable to the Anthropic/OpenAI ones. (All this being said, the international data center AIUI is in Singapore, which might have a slightly different hardware setup? I'm admittedly unsure of some of these details.)


I expect these costs for GLM5.2 to come down significantly over the coming months as well, as more optimisation is done to the serving stack(s).


I'm not sure how many major gains we'll see for 5.2 specifically, partly due to architecture (see below) but also because I'd be surprised if z.ai hasn't already optimized their kernels quite a bit, given that GLM-5.1-Highspeed already uses an optimized TileRT setup and have looked into newer networking setups (this might already be deployed somewhere on their systems, not sure).


They suggest that it is 2.75x cheaper per token to run inference on AMD vs Nvidia Blackwell.


I don't think this is what the article says? It's


At around 2.75x cheaper per GPU on average (MI355X vs B300) with comparable hardware specs,


Wafer's post is also a bit odd later on:


And again — on a 20k in / 1k out, 60% cache hit rate workload, we hit an aggregate throughput of 2626 tok/s/node @ 2.4 rps with a defined knee of ≤5s TTFT — only 80% of the performance measured on a B200,


Wait, why are we comparing to a B200 here? "only 80%" so is the MI355X slower than the B200, which is itself slower than the B300? Why is B300 being used for the price comparison then? Weird!

Also note that 5.2 is in general a bit expensive to run—at least when compared to other current open-weights models. It adopts DeepSeek V3.2's DSA, which improves "long-context" performance when you count around 64k as your long context...at the expense of increased memory usage by the KV cache. (You can see this on the KV cache calculator site, though it's not updated for 5.2 yet. But in a head-to-head at 1M context of K2.5 vs GLM 5, it's ~70GiB vs ~90GiB.) DSV4 has improved this substantially (see the charts in vLLM's article on this), but GLM's 5 line is still stuck on DSA, and although they've managed to reduce the overhead in 5.2 (see the "IndexShare" section of the blog post), we'll probably have to wait until a GLM 6 w/ a more V4-like architecture to bring the overhead down more.

On top of all of this, as you'd expect from an AI startup, z.ai is still running on at a loss:


Zhipu said in its earnings report released Tuesday that its revenue rose about 132% to 724 million yuan in 2025 from the previous year, though that figure missed the mean analyst estimate of 760 million yuan, polled by Reuters.

The firm reported a net adjusted loss of 3.18 billion yuan, up 29.1% from the previous year, as research and development spending increased.


Now, to be fair, this is a few months old now, but it would at least indicate that their R&D/training costs are still quite large. (Really I might expect it to have increased even more as of late, if they're chasing down something Fable-class in the coming year as they've hinted.) Given that they've already hiked inference costs when going from 5 -> 5.1, I don't think we can assume much of how their inference will cost in the future as they continue to scale up.

All of this is mostly just to say that I think the inference cost situation is still very fuzzy, in ways that make me hesitant to make much of a judgement on how the margins will fare as time passes.

comments.author: shanemhansen
comments.text:
I'm curious about other people's perspectives. I've been trying to use claude with open weight models. In particular deepseek 3.2 and zai GLM5.2. This was via amazon bedrock and openai compatible endpoints. With litellm proxy to do some tool calling fixing for deepseek.

The results were not great. Aside from the hacky fixes to make tool calling work sometimes in deepseek, it just didn't work reliably.

For GLM: I had what seemed to be genuinely terrible results. I used claude with opus and claude with glm. With glm aside from taking way longer, the code had terrible problems that glm was constantly fixing:


Missing double quotes in strings.

Imports in places that aren't syntactically allowed

Just bad looking code that violated best practices (storing a context variable in a struct).

non-sensical slop: a readLine function with timeout that just called another readLineOther function with timeout without changing the args, and the readLineOther function with timeout ignored the timeout argument and didn't implement the timeout.


opus code was less than 1/2 the loc of glm and this is subjective but every file passed that bar of "this is a good design, this was well written and even covers some things I didn't think of" vs GLM "this seems like crap code".

Am I missing something? Do people using GLM typically use a different harness or different verification skills? I want to use open weight models, but to me the differences in quality are obvious.

https://github.com/shanemhansen/claude-comparison

comments.author: bakkot
comments.text:
It's not obvious to me that "almost as good" implies "worth using" even at substantial savings. For anything I'm spending my own human effort on, it simply does not make sense to subject myself to stupider-than-necessary models in exchange for $20/mo (or whatever) in savings. I could definitely see using below-frontier models as a tool for your main AI to dispatch simpler tasks to, but not as the thing you'd actually be interacting with personally.

(This is not true at all margins: e.g. I will probably not be paying API prices for Fable for most tasks.)

comments.author: peter-leonov
comments.text:
True. But it also depends on your scale.

If it's a small group of devs solving different problems every day pushing a small number of products forward then a smarter more expensive model is fine.

On the other hand we have swarms of cheaper models doing the same stuff again and again like refactorings, greenfield bootsteapling, test coverage, etc. In a medium sized shop a 10x cheaper model will tip the scale a lot imo.

Secondly, and something I really didn't expect to be a blocker, is the lack of/poor web search capabilities. It turns out that nearly every agentic session does a lot of web searching for looking up items.
